chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: People who need rehabilitation after stroke should receive it from a specialist stroke service:

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: A core multidisciplinary stroke rehabilitation team should comprise the following professionals with expertise in stroke rehabilitation:

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: Throughout the care pathway, document the roles and responsibilities of the multidisciplinary team clearly and communicate these to the person and their family members and carers. [2013]

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: Health and social care professionals should collaborate to ensure a social care assessment is carried out promptly, where needed, before the person who has had a stroke is transferred from hospital to the community. The assessment should:

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: Offer training in care (for example, in how to move people and to help them with dressing) to family members and carers who are willing and able to be involved in supporting the person after stroke. [2013]

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: Review family members' and carers' training and support needs regularly (as a minimum at the person's 6-month and annual reviews), acknowledging that these needs may change over time. [2013]

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: Once the person has left hospital after having a stroke, continue their care and rehabilitation for as long as it continues to help them achieve their treatment goals. [2023]

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: Offer early supported discharge to people after stroke who can move from a bed to a chair independently or with assistance, as long as a safe and secure environment can be provided. [2013]

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: Before transfer from hospital to home or to a care setting, discuss and agree a health and social care plan with the person after stroke, and their family members and carers (as appropriate), and provide this to all relevant health and social care providers. [2013]

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: Before transfer of care from hospital to home:

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: On transfer of care from hospital to the community, provide information to all relevant health and social care professionals and the person after stroke. This should include a summary of the person's rehabilitation progress and current goals and details of their:

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: Ensure that people after stroke who are transferred from hospital to care homes receive assessment and treatment from stroke rehabilitation and social care services to the same standard as they would receive in their own homes. [2013]

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: Local health and social care providers should have standard operating procedures to ensure the safe transfer and long-term care of people after stroke, including those in care homes. This should include timely exchange of information between different providers using local protocols. [2013]

chunks.heading: Organising health and social care for people needing rehabilitation after stroke
chunks.excerpt: After transfer of care from hospital, people with rehabilitation needs after stroke (including those in care homes) should be followed up within 72 hours by the specialist stroke rehabilitation team to assess the needs of the person and develop shared management plans. [2013]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Perform a full medical assessment of the person after stroke, including cognition (attention, memory, spatial awareness, apraxia of speech , perception), vision, hearing, muscle tone, strength, sensation and balance. [2013]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: When collecting information from people who have had a stroke on admission and discharge:

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Take into account the impact of stroke on the person's family, friends and carers and, if appropriate, identify sources of support for them. [2013]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Inform the family members and carers of people after stroke about their right to a carer's needs assessment. [2013]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Ensure that people after stroke have goals for their rehabilitation that:

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: During goal-setting meetings, ensure people after stroke are provided with:

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Give people copies of their agreed goals for stroke rehabilitation after each goal-setting meeting. [2013]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Review people's goals at regular intervals during their stroke rehabilitation. [2013]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Provide information and support to enable the person after stroke and their family members and carers (as appropriate) to actively take part in developing their stroke rehabilitation plan. [2013]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Review stroke rehabilitation plans regularly in multidisciplinary team meetings. Time these reviews according to the stage of rehabilitation and the person's needs. [2013]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Ensure any documentation is tailored to the person after stroke and, as a minimum, includes:

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: For information on high-intensity mobilisation during the first 24 hours after the onset of stroke symptoms, see recommendation 1.7.3 in the section on early mobilisation in NICE's guideline on stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s . [2023]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Offer needs-based rehabilitation to people after stroke. This should be for at least 3 hours a day, on at least 5 days of the week, and cover a range of multidisciplinary therapy including physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy. [2023]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Where it is agreed with the person after stroke that they are unable, or do not wish, to participate in rehabilitation therapy for at least 3 hours a day, on at least 5 days of the week, ensure that any therapy needed is still offered for a minimum of 5 days per week. [2023]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Involve families and carers in rehabilitation sessions, when appropriate (see NICE's guideline on patient experience in adult NHS services ). [2023]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Make special arrangements for people after stroke who have communication or cognitive needs (for example, by holding joint speech and language therapy and physiotherapy sessions for those with communication difficulties). [2023]

chunks.heading: Planning and delivering stroke rehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: When planning or delivering rehabilitation for people after they have left hospital:

chunks.excerpt: Consider telerehabilitation instead of, or as well as, face-to-face therapy, only if:

chunks.heading: Telerehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Ensure that anyone taking part in telerehabilitation has, or when needed is provided with, the correct equipment (for example, a loaned laptop) and any training or technical support they need to use it. [2023]

chunks.heading: Telerehabilitation
chunks.excerpt: Monitor people who are taking part in telerehabilitation to ensure they are:

chunks.heading: Providing support and information
chunks.excerpt: Work with the person after stroke, and their family members and carers, to identify their information needs and how to deliver this information. Take into account any specific impairments such as aphasia (loss or impairment of the ability to use and comprehend language) and cognitive impairments. Pace the way information is given to allow time for the person to make an emotional adjustment. [2013]

chunks.heading: Providing support and information
chunks.excerpt: Provide information about local resources (for example, leisure, housing, social services and voluntary organisations) that can help support the needs and priorities of the person after stroke and their family members and carers. [2013]

chunks.heading: Providing support and information
chunks.excerpt: Review the person's information needs at their 6-month and annual stroke reviews, and at the start and end of any therapy. [2013]

chunks.heading: Cognitive functioning
chunks.excerpt: Screen people after stroke for cognitive impairment. Where cognitive impairment is identified, carry out a detailed assessment using valid, reliable and responsive tools before designing a treatment programme. [2013]

chunks.heading: Cognitive functioning
chunks.excerpt: Provide education and support for people after stroke, and their families and carers, to help them understand the extent and impact of cognitive impairment, recognising that these may vary over time and in different settings. [2013]

chunks.heading: Cognitive functioning
chunks.excerpt: Use standardised assessments and behavioural observation to assess the effect of visual inattention (an inability to orient towards and attend to stimuli, including body parts, on the side of the body affected by stroke) on functional tasks such as mobility, dressing, eating and using a wheelchair. [2013]

chunks.heading: Cognitive functioning
chunks.excerpt: Use interventions for visual inattention that focus on the relevant functional tasks, taking into account the underlying impairment. For example:

chunks.heading: Cognitive functioning
chunks.excerpt: Assess memory and other relevant domains of cognitive functioning (such as executive functions) in people after stroke, particularly where impairments in memory affect everyday activity. [2013]

chunks.heading: Cognitive functioning
chunks.excerpt: Use interventions for memory and cognitive functions that focus on the relevant functional tasks, taking into account the underlying impairment. Interventions could include:

chunks.heading: Cognitive functioning
chunks.excerpt: Assess attention and cognitive functions in people after stroke using standardised assessments. Use behavioural observation to evaluate the impact of any impairment on functional tasks. [2013]

chunks.heading: Cognitive functioning
chunks.excerpt: Consider attention training for people with attention deficits after stroke. [2013]

chunks.heading: Cognitive functioning
chunks.excerpt: Use interventions for attention and cognitive functions after stroke that focus on the relevant functional tasks. For example, by minimising distractions and providing prompts related to the task. [2013]

chunks.heading: Psychological functioning
chunks.excerpt: Assess the person after stroke for changes to:

chunks.heading: Psychological functioning
chunks.excerpt: When choosing any intervention for problems with emotional functioning, take into account the type or complexity of the person's neuropsychological presentation and relevant personal history. [2013]

chunks.heading: Psychological functioning
chunks.excerpt: Support and educate people and their families and carers to help them make an emotional adjustment after stroke, recognising that their psychological needs may change over time and in different settings. [2013]

chunks.heading: Psychological functioning
chunks.excerpt: When new or persisting changes to mood or emotional difficulties are identified at the person's 6-month or annual stroke review, refer them to appropriate services for detailed assessment and treatment. [2013]

chunks.heading: Psychological functioning
chunks.excerpt: Manage depression or anxiety in people after stroke who have no cognitive impairment in line with NICE's guidelines on depression in adults with a chronic physical health problem and generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults . [2013]

chunks.heading: Fatigue
chunks.excerpt: Consider a standardised assessment for fatigue in people after stroke in the early stage of their rehabilitation programme and at their 6-month stroke review. [2023]

chunks.heading: Fatigue
chunks.excerpt: Consider 1 of the following for the assessment:

chunks.heading: Vision
chunks.excerpt: Offer people who are in hospital after stroke a specialist orthoptist assessment as soon as possible. If this cannot be done before discharge, offer the person an urgent outpatient appointment. [2023]

chunks.heading: Vision
chunks.excerpt: Offer eye movement therapy to people who have persisting hemianopia (blindness in 1 half of the visual field of 1 or both eyes) after stroke. [2013, amended 2023]

chunks.heading: Vision
chunks.excerpt: When advising people with visual problems after stroke about driving, consult the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) regulations . [2013]

chunks.heading: Hearing
chunks.excerpt: Screen people for hearing problems within the first 6 weeks after stroke. [2023]

chunks.heading: Hearing
chunks.excerpt: Consider the Handicap Hearing Inventory in the Elderly or Amsterdam Inventory Auditory of Disability questionnaires for screening. [2023]

chunks.heading: Hearing
chunks.excerpt: During screening, ask the person, and their family members and carers, about any changes to their hearing since the stroke. [2023]

chunks.heading: Hearing
chunks.excerpt: Refer people with hearing difficulties for an audiology assessment, in line with NICE's guideline on hearing loss in adults . [2023]

chunks.heading: Mouth care
chunks.excerpt: Assess oral hygiene in people after stroke using national or local protocols. [2023]

chunks.heading: Mouth care
chunks.excerpt: Encourage people after stroke to do the following at least twice a day:

chunks.heading: Mouth care
chunks.excerpt: Ensure that a suitably trained healthcare professional, family member or carer delivers or supervises mouth care for people after stroke who cannot, or find it difficult to, follow a mouth care regimen. [2023]

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: Assess swallowing in people after stroke in line with NICE's guideline on stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s . [2013]

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: Provide information to people with dysphagia (difficulty in swallowing) after stroke, and their families and carers, on what the condition is and its risks. [2023]

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: Give families and carers information on how they can help someone who is coughing or choking while eating or drinking. [2023]

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: If the person has dysphagia and is unable to take tablets, review the need for the medication and, if it is still needed, change either its formulation or the route of administration. [2023]

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: Support people who have oropharyngeal dysphagia (OPD) to eat and drink as safely as possible, using 1 or more of the following methods (as advised by a dysphagia-trained healthcare professional):

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: Offer behavioural exercises (for example, chin tuck against resistance) to people with OPD for at least 5 days per week. [2023]

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: Consider physical stimulation (for example, thermal or tactile stimulation) for people with OPD for at least 5 days per week. [2023]

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: Ensure people with dysphagia after stroke are supported in following an effective mouth care regimen, because this decreases the risk of aspiration pneumonia (see the section on mouth care ). [2013]

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: Healthcare professionals with relevant skills and training in the diagnosis, assessment and management of swallowing disorders should regularly monitor and reassess people with dysphagia after stroke who are having modified food and liquid until they are stable (this recommendation is from NICE's guideline on nutrition support for adults ). [2013]

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: Provide nutrition support to people with dysphagia in line with NICE's guidelines on nutrition support for adults and stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s . [2013]

chunks.heading: Swallowing
chunks.excerpt: If the person with dysphagia is at risk of aspiration but wishes to eat and drink without the assistance of aids and interventions (such as the methods listed in recommendations 1.11.5 to 1.11.7 for people with OPD):

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Screen people for communication difficulties within 72 hours of onset of stroke symptoms. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Each stroke rehabilitation service should devise a standardised protocol to screen for communication difficulties in people after stroke. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Refer people with suspected communication difficulties after stroke to a speech and language therapist for detailed analysis of any impairments and assessment of their impact. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Provide appropriate information, education and training to the multidisciplinary team to enable them to support and communicate effectively with people who have communication difficulties and their families and carers. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Speech and language therapy for people after stroke should be led and supervised by a specialist speech and language therapist working collaboratively with other appropriately trained people (for example, speech and language therapy assistants, carers and friends, or members of the voluntary sector). [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Provide opportunities for people with communication difficulties after stroke to have conversations and social contact with people who have the training, knowledge, skills and behaviours to support them. This should be in addition to the opportunities provided by families, carers and friends. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Speech and language therapists should assess people experiencing severe communication difficulties after stroke to see if they could benefit from using a communication aid or other technologies (for example, home-based computer therapies or mobile apps). [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Consider a computer-based programme (or apps) tailored to individual goals and circumstances in relation to word finding, alongside face-to-face speech and language therapy. [2023]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Provide communication aids to people who could benefit from them after stroke and offer training in how to use them. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Tell people with communication difficulties after stroke about community-based communication and support groups (such as those provided by voluntary organisations) and encourage them to participate in them. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: When persisting communication difficulties are identified at the person's 6-month or annual stroke review, refer them back to a speech and language therapist for detailed assessment, and offer treatment if they could benefit from it. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Help and enable people with communication difficulties after stroke to express their everyday needs and wishes, and support them to understand and participate in both everyday and major life decisions. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Ensure that environmental barriers to communication are minimised for people after stroke. For example, make sure signage is clear and background noise is limited. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Make sure that all written information (including that relating to medical conditions and treatment) is adapted for people with aphasia after stroke. This should include, for example, appointment letters, rehabilitation timetables and menus. [2013]

chunks.heading: Communication
chunks.excerpt: Offer training in communication skills (such as slowing down, not interrupting and using communication props, gestures or drawing) to those who regularly communicate with people who have aphasia after stroke. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Provide physiotherapy for people after stroke who have weakness in their trunk or upper or lower limbs, sensory disturbance or balance difficulties that affect their movement. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: People with movement difficulties after stroke should be treated by physiotherapists with the relevant skills and training in diagnosis, assessment and management. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Continue to treat people with movement difficulties until they are able to maintain or progress function either independently or with assistance from others (for example, rehabilitation assistants, family members, carers or fitness instructors). [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Consider strength training for people with muscle weakness after stroke. This could include progressive strength building through increasing repetitions of body weight activities (for example, sit-to-stand repetitions), weights (for example, progressive resistance exercise), or resistance exercise on machines such as stationary cycles. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Encourage people to participate in physical activity after stroke. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Assess people who are able to walk and are medically stable after stroke for cardiorespiratory and resistance training that is appropriate to their individual goals. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Cardiorespiratory and resistance training for people after stroke should be started by a physiotherapist who can give them instructions on how to continue the programme independently. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: If people after stroke choose to continue with an exercise programme independently, ensure physiotherapists supply any necessary information about interventions and adaptations to the provider so they can make sure the programme is:

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Tell people who are participating in fitness activities after stroke about common, potential problems, such as shoulder pain, and advise them to seek advice from their GP or therapist if these occur. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Do not routinely offer wrist and hand splints to people with upper limb weakness after stroke. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Consider wrist and hand splints for people at risk after stroke (for example, people who have hands that are immobile due to weakness or high tone), to:

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Ensure wrist and hand splints used by people after stroke are fitted by appropriately trained healthcare professionals, and a review plan is established. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Teach the person after stroke, and their family members and carers, how to put the splint on and take it off, care for it and monitor for signs of redness and skin breakdown. Provide a point of contact for the person if concerned. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Do not routinely offer people after stroke electrical stimulation for their hand or arm. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Consider a trial of electrical stimulation therapy as part of a comprehensive rehabilitation programme for people who have evidence of muscle contraction after stroke but cannot move their arm against resistance. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Continue electrical stimulation therapy if the person's strength and their ability to practise functional tasks (for example, maintaining range of movement, or improving grasp and release) is found to be improving. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: If a trial of electrical stimulation therapy is appropriate, ensure the treatment is guided by a qualified rehabilitation professional. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Do not offer robot-assisted arm training as part of an upper limb rehabilitation programme. [2023]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Consider constraint-induced movement therapy for people after stroke who have movement of 20 degrees of wrist extension and 10 degrees of finger extension. Be aware of potential adverse events (such as falls, low mood and fatigue). [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Offer people after stroke repetitive task training on a range of activities for upper limb weakness (such as tasks that involve reaching, grasping, pointing, moving and manipulating objects) and lower limb weakness (such as sit-to-stand transfers, walking and using stairs). [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Offer walking training to people after stroke who are able to walk, with or without assistance, to help them build endurance and move more quickly. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Consider treadmill training, with or without body weight support, as an option for people after stroke who are able to walk with or without assistance. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: In addition to one-to-one walking therapy for people after stroke who are able to walk, with or without assistance, consider a programme of group circuit training that:

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Offer electromechanical gait training to people after stroke only in the context of a research study. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Consider ankle–foot orthoses (devices that support or correct limb function) for people who have difficulty with swing-phase foot clearance after stroke (for example, tripping and falling) or stance-phase control (for example, knee and ankle collapse or knee hyper-extensions) that affects walking. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Assess the ability of the person to put on the ankle–foot orthosis or ensure they have the support needed to do so. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Assess the effectiveness of the ankle–foot orthosis for the person, in terms of comfort, speed and ease of walking. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Assessment for and treatment with ankle–foot orthoses should only be carried out as part of a stroke rehabilitation programme and performed by qualified professionals. [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Follow NICE's interventional procedures guidance on functional electrical stimulation for drop foot of central neurological origin . [2013]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: Consider mirror therapy for people with muscle weakness in their upper or lower limbs after a stroke as an adjunct to their rehabilitation programme. [2023]

chunks.heading: Movement
chunks.excerpt: If provided, start mirror therapy within the first 6 months after a stroke. Sessions should be:

chunks.heading: Managing shoulder pain
chunks.excerpt: Provide information for people after stroke, and their families and carers, on how to prevent pain or trauma to the shoulder if they are at risk of developing shoulder pain (for example, if they have upper limb weakness and spasticity). [2013]

chunks.heading: Managing shoulder pain
chunks.excerpt: Assess people with shoulder pain after stroke to identify its cause and use the results of the assessment to decide how to manage the pain. [2023]

chunks.heading: Managing shoulder pain
chunks.excerpt: Encourage or help the person to adapt their position to help ease shoulder pain. [2013, amended 2023]

chunks.heading: Managing shoulder pain
chunks.excerpt: Consider 1 or more of the following options for managing shoulder pain:

chunks.heading: Spasticity
chunks.excerpt: Provide information on spasticity for people after stroke, and their families and carers, including details about what it is and what can make it better or worse. [2023]

chunks.heading: Spasticity
chunks.excerpt: Assess whether spasticity in people after stroke is focal (that is, it affects a specific limb or part of a limb) or generalised. [2023]

chunks.heading: Spasticity
chunks.excerpt: Discuss options for managing focal or generalised spasticity in the person after stroke with the multidisciplinary team. [2023]

chunks.heading: Spasticity
chunks.excerpt: Consider 1 or more of the following as part of a goal-directed plan to manage focal or generalised spasticity in people after stroke:

chunks.heading: Spasticity
chunks.excerpt: For people who have focal spasticity of the upper limb after stroke, consider treatment with either Dysport at a dose of up to 1,000 units per treatment or with Xeomin at a dose of up to 400 units per treatment, unless they are already receiving a different type or dose of botulinum toxin A. Ensure that:

chunks.heading: Spasticity
chunks.excerpt: Consider a trial of NMES, functional electrical stimulation (FES) or transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) for people after stroke with focal spasticity. [2023]

chunks.heading: Spasticity
chunks.excerpt: Consider oral baclofen for people after stroke with generalised spasticity but monitor closely for adverse effects. [2023]

chunks.heading: Spasticity
chunks.excerpt: Refer people after stroke to a specialist spasticity service if:

chunks.heading: Self-care
chunks.excerpt: Provide occupational therapy for people after stroke who are likely to benefit from it and to address difficulties with activities of daily living. Therapy may consist of restorative or compensatory strategies.

chunks.heading: Self-care
chunks.excerpt: People who have difficulties with activities of daily living after stroke should have regular monitoring and treatment by occupational therapists with core skills and training in the analysis and management of activities of daily living. Treatment should continue until the person's condition is stable or able to progress independently. [2013]

chunks.heading: Self-care
chunks.excerpt: Assess people after stroke for their equipment needs and to see whether their family or carers need training to use the equipment. This assessment should be done by an appropriately qualified professional. Equipment may include hoists, chair raisers and small aids such as long-handled sponges. [2013]

chunks.heading: Self-care
chunks.excerpt: Identify any return-to-work issues for the person as soon as possible after stroke. Review these regularly and manage them actively, for example by:

chunks.heading: Self-care
chunks.excerpt: Consider a referral to a return-to-work programme for people who were working before they had a stroke. [2023]

chunks.heading: Self-care
chunks.excerpt: Manage people's return to work or long-term absence after stroke in line with NICE's guideline on workplace health . [2013]

chunks.heading: Long-term health and social support
chunks.excerpt: Explain to people after stroke that they can self-refer, usually with the support from a health or care professional working in primary care (for example, a GP or a social prescriber) or named contact from the stroke rehabilitation service, if they need further help or support. [2013]

chunks.heading: Long-term health and social support
chunks.excerpt: Provide information so that people after stroke, and their family and carers, can recognise the complications of the condition, including frequent falls, spasticity, shoulder pain and incontinence. [2013]

chunks.heading: Long-term health and social support
chunks.excerpt: Encourage people to focus on life after stroke and help them to achieve their goals. This may include:

chunks.heading: Long-term health and social support
chunks.excerpt: Manage incontinence after stroke in line with NICE's guidelines on urinary incontinence in neurological disease and faecal incontinence in adults . [2013]

chunks.heading: Long-term health and social support
chunks.excerpt: Review the health and social care needs of people after stroke, and the needs of their carers, at 6 months and then annually. These reviews should cover participation in activities of everyday life to ensure that people's goals are met. [2013]

chunks.heading: Long-term health and social support
chunks.excerpt: Consider referral for people after stroke, and their families and carers (if appropriate), to community participation programmes that:

chunks.heading: Rapid recognition of symptoms and diagnosis
chunks.excerpt: Use a validated tool, such as FAST (Face Arm Speech Test), outside hospital to screen people with sudden onset of neurological symptoms for a diagnosis of stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). [2008]

chunks.heading: Rapid recognition of symptoms and diagnosis
chunks.excerpt: Exclude hypoglycaemia in people with sudden onset of neurological symptoms as the cause of these symptoms. [2008]

chunks.heading: Rapid recognition of symptoms and diagnosis
chunks.excerpt: For people who are admitted to the emergency department with a suspected stroke or TIA, establish the diagnosis rapidly using a validated tool, such as ROSIER (Recognition of Stroke in the Emergency Room). [2008]

chunks.heading: Rapid recognition of symptoms and diagnosis
chunks.excerpt: Offer aspirin (300 mg daily), unless contraindicated, to people who have had a suspected TIA, to be started immediately. [2019]

chunks.heading: Rapid recognition of symptoms and diagnosis
chunks.excerpt: Refer immediately people who have had a suspected TIA for specialist assessment and investigation, to be seen within 24 hours of onset of symptoms. [2019]

chunks.heading: Rapid recognition of symptoms and diagnosis
chunks.excerpt: Do not use scoring systems, such as ABCD2, to assess risk of subsequent stroke or to inform urgency of referral for people who have had a suspected or confirmed TIA. [2019]

chunks.heading: Rapid recognition of symptoms and diagnosis
chunks.excerpt: Offer secondary prevention, in addition to aspirin, as soon as possible after the diagnosis of TIA is confirmed. [2008, amended 2019]

chunks.heading: Imaging for people who have had a suspected TIA or acute non-disabling stroke
chunks.excerpt: Do not offer CT brain scanning to people with a suspected TIA unless there is clinical suspicion of an alternative diagnosis that CT could detect. [2019]

chunks.heading: Imaging for people who have had a suspected TIA or acute non-disabling stroke
chunks.excerpt: After specialist assessment in the TIA clinic, consider MRI (including diffusion-weighted and blood-sensitive sequences) to determine the territory of ischaemia, or to detect haemorrhage or alternative pathologies. If MRI is done, perform it on the same day as the assessment. [2019]

chunks.heading: Imaging for people who have had a suspected TIA or acute non-disabling stroke
chunks.excerpt: Everyone with TIA who after specialist assessment is considered as a candidate for carotid endarterectomy should have urgent carotid imaging. [2008, amended 2019]

chunks.heading: Imaging for people who have had a suspected TIA or acute non-disabling stroke
chunks.excerpt: Ensure that people with stable neurological symptoms from acute non-disabling stroke or TIA who have symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50% to 99% according to the NASCET (North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial) criteria:

chunks.heading: Imaging for people who have had a suspected TIA or acute non-disabling stroke
chunks.excerpt: Ensure that people with stable neurological symptoms from acute non-disabling stroke or TIA who have symptomatic carotid stenosis of less than 50% according to the NASCET criteria, or less than 70% according to the European Carotid Surgery Trial (ECST) criteria:

chunks.heading: Imaging for people who have had a suspected TIA or acute non-disabling stroke
chunks.excerpt: Ensure that carotid imaging reports clearly state which criteria (ECST or NASCET) were used when measuring the extent of carotid stenosis. [2008]

chunks.heading: Specialist care for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Admit everyone with suspected stroke directly to a specialist acute stroke unit after initial assessment, from either the community, the emergency department, or outpatient clinics. (An acute stroke unit is a discrete area in the hospital that is staffed by a specialist stroke multidisciplinary team. It has access to equipment for monitoring and rehabilitating patients. Regular multidisciplinary team meetings occur for goal setting.). [2008]

chunks.heading: Specialist care for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Perform brain imaging immediately with a non-enhanced CT for people with suspected acute stroke if any of the following apply (see additional information ):

chunks.heading: Specialist care for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Perform scanning as soon as possible and within 24 hours of symptom onset in everyone with suspected acute stroke without indications for immediate brain imaging. [2008]

chunks.excerpt: Alteplase is recommended within its marketing authorisation for treating acute ischaemic stroke in adults if:

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Administer alteplase only within a well-organised stroke service with:

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Staff in emergency departments, if appropriately trained and supported, can administer alteplase for the treatment of ischaemic stroke provided that patients can be managed within an acute stroke service with appropriate neuroradiological and stroke physician support. [2008]

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Ensure that protocols are in place for delivering and managing intravenous thrombolysis, including post-thrombolysis complications. [2008]

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Offer thrombectomy as soon as possible and within 6 hours of symptom onset, together with intravenous thrombolysis (if not contraindicated and within the licensed time window), to people who have:

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Offer a proton pump inhibitor, in addition to aspirin, to anyone with acute ischaemic stroke for whom previous dyspepsia associated with aspirin is reported. [2008]

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Offer an alternative antiplatelet agent to anyone with acute ischaemic stroke who is allergic to or genuinely intolerant of aspirin. (Aspirin intolerance is defined as either of the following: proven hypersensitivity to aspirin-containing medicines, or history of severe dyspepsia induced by low-dose aspirin.) [2008]

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Do not use anticoagulation treatment routinely for the treatment of acute stroke (see additional information ). [2008]

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: For people with prosthetic valves who have disabling cerebral infarction and who are at significant risk of haemorrhagic transformation, stop anticoagulation treatment for 1 week and substitute aspirin 300 mg. [2008]

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Ensure that people with ischaemic stroke and symptomatic proximal deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism receive anticoagulation treatment in preference to treatment with aspirin unless there are other contraindications to anticoagulation. [2008]

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Treat people who have haemorrhagic stroke and symptomatic deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism to prevent the development of further pulmonary emboli using either anticoagulation or a caval filter. [2008]

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Immediate initiation of statin treatment is not recommended in people with acute stroke (see additional information ). [2008]

chunks.heading: Pharmacological treatments and thrombectomy for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Continue statin treatment in people with acute stroke who are already receiving statins. [2008]

chunks.heading: Maintenance or restoration of homeostasis
chunks.excerpt: Give supplemental oxygen to people who have had a stroke only if their oxygen saturation drops below 95%. The routine use of supplemental oxygen is not recommended in people with acute stroke who are not hypoxic. [2008]

chunks.heading: Maintenance or restoration of homeostasis
chunks.excerpt: Maintain a blood glucose concentration between 4 and 11 mmol/litre in people with acute stroke. [2008]

chunks.heading: Maintenance or restoration of homeostasis
chunks.excerpt: Provide optimal insulin therapy, which can be achieved by the use of intravenous insulin and glucose, to all adults with type 1 diabetes with threatened or actual stroke. Critical care and emergency departments should have a protocol for such management. [2008]

chunks.heading: Maintenance or restoration of homeostasis
chunks.excerpt: Consider rapid blood pressure lowering for people with acute intracerebral haemorrhage who do not have any of the exclusions listed in recommendation 1.5.7 and who:

chunks.heading: Maintenance or restoration of homeostasis
chunks.excerpt: Taking into account the risk of harm, consider rapid blood pressure lowering on a case-by-case basis for people with acute intracerebral haemorrhage who do not have any of the exclusions listed in recommendation 1.5.7 and who:

chunks.heading: Maintenance or restoration of homeostasis
chunks.excerpt: When rapidly lowering blood pressure in people with acute intracerebral haemorrhage, aim to reach a systolic blood pressure of 140 mmHg or lower while ensuring that the magnitude drop does not exceed 60 mmHg within 1 hour of starting treatment. [2022]

chunks.excerpt: When considering blood pressure lowering in young people aged 16 or 17 with acute intracerebral haemorrhage who do not have any of the exclusions listed in recommendation 1.5.7 , seek advice from a paediatric specialist. [2022]

chunks.heading: Maintenance or restoration of homeostasis
chunks.excerpt: Blood pressure reduction to 185/110 mmHg or lower should be considered in people who are candidates for intravenous thrombolysis. [2008]

chunks.heading: Nutrition and hydration
chunks.excerpt: On admission, ensure that people with acute stroke have their swallowing screened by an appropriately trained healthcare professional before being given any oral food, fluid or medication. [2008]

chunks.heading: Nutrition and hydration
chunks.excerpt: If the admission screen indicates problems with swallowing, ensure that the person has a specialist assessment of swallowing, preferably within 24 hours of admission and not more than 72 hours afterwards. [2008]

chunks.excerpt: People with suspected aspiration on specialist assessment, or who require tube feeding or dietary modification for 3 days, should be:

chunks.heading: Nutrition and hydration
chunks.excerpt: People with acute stroke who are unable to take adequate nutrition, fluids and medication orally should:

chunks.heading: Nutrition and hydration
chunks.excerpt: Screen all hospital inpatients on admission for malnutrition and the risk of malnutrition. Repeat screening weekly for inpatients. [2008]

chunks.heading: Nutrition and hydration
chunks.excerpt: Screening should assess body mass index (BMI) and percentage unintentional weight loss. It should also consider the time over which a nutrient intake has been unintentionally reduced and/or the likelihood of future impaired nutrient intake. The Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), for example, may be used to do this. [2008]

chunks.heading: Nutrition and hydration
chunks.excerpt: When screening for malnutrition and the risk of malnutrition, be aware that dysphagia, poor oral health and reduced ability to self-feed will affect nutrition in people with stroke. [2008]

chunks.heading: Nutrition and hydration
chunks.excerpt: Screening for malnutrition and the risk of malnutrition should be carried out by healthcare professionals with appropriate skills and training. [2008]

chunks.heading: Nutrition and hydration
chunks.excerpt: Routine nutritional supplementation is not recommended for people with acute stroke who are adequately nourished on admission. [2008]

chunks.heading: Nutrition and hydration
chunks.excerpt: Start nutrition support for people with stroke who are at risk of malnutrition. This may include oral nutritional supplements, specialist dietary advice and/or tube feeding. [2008]

chunks.heading: Nutrition and hydration
chunks.excerpt: Assess, on admission, the hydration of everyone with acute stroke. Review hydration regularly and manage it so that normal hydration is maintained. [2008]

chunks.heading: Optimal positioning and early mobilisation for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Assess the individual clinical needs and personal preferences of people with acute stroke to determine their optimal head position. Take into account factors such as their comfort, physical and cognitive abilities and postural control. [2019]

chunks.heading: Optimal positioning and early mobilisation for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Help people with acute stroke to sit out of bed, stand or walk as soon as their clinical condition permits as part of an active management programme in a specialist stroke unit. [2019]

chunks.heading: Optimal positioning and early mobilisation for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: If people need help to sit out of bed, stand or walk, do not offer high-intensity mobilisation in the first 24 hours after symptom onset. [2019]

chunks.heading: Avoiding aspiration pneumonia
chunks.excerpt: To avoid aspiration pneumonia, give food, fluids and medication to people with dysphagia in a form that can be swallowed without aspiration, after specialist assessment of swallowing (see recommendation 1.6.2 ). [2008]

chunks.heading: Surgery for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Stroke services should agree protocols for monitoring, referring and transferring people to regional neurosurgical centres for the management of symptomatic hydrocephalus. [2008]

chunks.heading: Surgery for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: People with intracerebral haemorrhage should be monitored by specialists in neurosurgical or stroke care for deterioration in function and referred immediately for brain imaging when necessary. [2008]

chunks.heading: Surgery for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Previously fit people should be considered for surgical intervention following primary intracerebral haemorrhage if they have hydrocephalus. [2008]

chunks.heading: Surgery for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: People with any of the following rarely require surgical intervention and should receive medical treatment initially:

chunks.heading: Surgery for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Consider decompressive hemicraniectomy (which should be performed within 48 hours of symptom onset) for people with acute stroke who meet all of the following criteria:

chunks.heading: Surgery for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: Discuss the risks and benefits of decompressive hemicraniectomy with people or their family members or carers (as appropriate), taking into account their functional status before the stroke, and their wishes and preferences. [2019]

chunks.heading: Surgery for people with acute stroke
chunks.excerpt: People who are referred for decompressive hemicraniectomy should be monitored by appropriately trained professionals skilled in neurological assessment. [2008]

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Healthcare professionals should adapt their consultation style to the needs of individual patients so that all patients have the opportunity to be involved in decisions about their medicines at the level they wish.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Consider any factors such as physical or learning disabilities, sight or hearing problems and difficulties with reading or speaking English, which may affect the patient's involvement in the consultation.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Establish the most effective way of communicating with each patient and, if necessary, consider ways of making information accessible and understandable (for example, using pictures, symbols, large print, different languages, an interpreter or a patient advocate).

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Encourage patients to ask about their condition and treatment.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Ask patients open˗ended questions because these are more likely to uncover patients' concerns.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Be aware that the consultation skills needed for increasing patient involvement can be improved.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Offer all patients the opportunity to be involved in making decisions about prescribed medicines. Establish what level of involvement in decision-making the patient would like.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Discuss with the patient why they might benefit from the treatment. Clearly explain the disease or condition and how the medicine will influence this.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Explain the medical aims of the treatment to patients and openly discuss the pros and cons of proposed medicines. The discussion should be at the level preferred by the patient.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Clarify what the patient hopes the treatment will achieve.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Avoid making assumptions about patient preferences about treatment. Talk to the patient to find out their preferences, and note any non˗verbal cues that may indicate you need to explore the patient's perspective further.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Healthcare professionals have a duty to help patients to make decisions about their treatment based on an understanding of the likely benefits and risks rather than on misconceptions.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Accept that patients may have different views from healthcare professionals about the balance of risks, benefits and side effects of medicines.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Be aware that increasing patient involvement may mean that the patient decides not to take or to stop taking a medicine. If in the healthcare professional's view this could have an adverse effect, then the information provided to the patient on risks and benefits and the patient's decision should be recorded.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Accept that the patient has the right to decide not to take a medicine, even if you do not agree with the decision, as long as the patient has the capacity to make an informed decision and has been provided with the information needed to make such a decision.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: If the patient has specific concerns, record a summary of the discussion, because this may be helpful in future consultations.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Encourage and support patients, families and carers to keep an up˗to˗date list of all medicines the patient is taking. The list should include the names and dosages of prescription and non˗prescription medicines and herbal and nutritional supplements. If the patient has any allergic or adverse reactions to medicines, these should be noted.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Be aware that patients' concerns about medicines, and whether they believe they need them, affect how and whether they take their prescribed medicines.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Ask patients what they know, believe and understand about medicines before prescribing new treatments and when reviewing medicines.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Ask if the patient has any specific concerns about their medicines, whenever you prescribe, dispense or review medicines. These may include concerns about becoming dependent on medicines and concerns about adverse effects. Address these concerns.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Be aware that patients may wish to minimise how much medicine they take.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Offer patients information about medicines before the medicines are prescribed.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Offer patients information that is relevant to their condition, possible treatments and personal circumstances, and that is easy to understand and free from jargon.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Check that patients have any information they wish about medicines when the medicines are dispensed.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Discuss information on medicines with the patient rather than just presenting it. The discussion should take into account what the patient understands and believes about the condition and treatment.

chunks.heading: Patient involvement in decisions about medicines
chunks.excerpt: Do not assume that the patient information leaflets (PILs) that patients receive with their medicines will meet each patient's needs. Address concerns that patients may have after reading the standard PILs.

chunks.heading: Supporting adherence
chunks.excerpt: Recognise that non˗adherence is common and that most patients are non˗adherent sometimes. Routinely assess adherence in a non˗judgemental way whenever you prescribe, dispense and review medicines.

chunks.heading: Supporting adherence

chunks.heading: Supporting adherence
chunks.excerpt: Consider using records of prescription re˗ordering, pharmacy patient medication records and return of unused medicines to identify potential non˗adherence and patients needing additional support.

chunks.heading: Supporting adherence
chunks.excerpt: If a patient is not taking their medicines, discuss with them whether this is because of beliefs and concerns or problems about the medicines (intentional non˗adherence) or because of practical problems (unintentional non˗adherence).

chunks.heading: Supporting adherence
chunks.excerpt: Be aware that although adherence can be improved, no specific intervention can be recommended for all patients. Tailor any intervention to increase adherence to the specific difficulties with adherence the patient is experiencing.

chunks.heading: Supporting adherence
chunks.excerpt: Find out what form of support the patient would prefer to increase their adherence to medicines. Together, you and your patient should consider options for support.

chunks.heading: Supporting adherence
chunks.excerpt: Address any beliefs and concerns that patients have that result in reduced adherence.
